claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed native surface oxide layer.
The native oxide layer governs Q235 corrosion resistance at both room temperature and 700–900 °C.
Annealing a preserved native oxide produces a continuous, dense, and adherent protective film on Q235 steel.
A continuous, dense oxide film retards transport of corrosive species and further oxidation.
The evolved oxide film limits salt access and elemental dissolution from Q235 steel.
Removing or disrupting the native oxide before annealing prevents formation of a coherent protective scale.
Removal or annealing-induced degradation of the native oxide causes increased corrosion and mass loss.
Annealing promotes diffusion and re-oxidation that converts the pre-existing oxide into a dense, adherent film.
Oxide-preserved samples will exhibit lower mass loss than oxide-removed samples after high-temperature salt exposure.
Oxide-preserved samples will show fewer microstructural indications of salt penetration than oxide-removed samples.
Oxide-preserved samples will have greater corrosion resistance than oxide-removed samples, especially at high temperature.
As-received Q235 with an unaltered native oxide has moderate room-temperature corrosion resistance.
Optimally annealed Q235 with an unaltered native oxide has enhanced corrosion protection.
The proposed native-oxide mechanism is significant during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
The effect of native-oxide evolution is less pronounced under ambient conditions because corrosion kinetics are slower.
Protective oxide layers can be unstable in molten fluoride salts, allowing dissolution of the least noble alloy element.
Oxide integrity, density, and adhesion are the structural variables mediating corrosion protection.
No significant difference in mass change, oxide integrity, or salt penetration between oxide-preserved and oxide-removed samples would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says the native oxide governs protection in both room- and high-temperature regimes, while the conditions state that protection is expected only when the oxide evolves under the high-temperature regime. The boundary later weakens this to a merely less-pronounced ambient effect.

The intervention specifies annealing under inert conditions, whereas the mechanism invokes annealing-promoted re-oxidation. Re-oxidation requires an oxidant or controlled oxygen potential that the design does not specify.
